reads.worst: The final rating infers honesty from transparent reply-pattern heuristics, so unusual but honest wording can be scored incorrectly.

reads.best: A single actionable queue addresses the practical bottleneck of supervising multiple Hermes runs while keeping decisions with the person.
reads.worst: Queue detection uses language heuristics and private Kanban/database interfaces, while automatic summaries send cross-profile item text to the configured model by default.

reads.best: A new channel between agents with strong safety design: the inbox is untrusted (the model sees only counts), sending needs a human, there are about 33 MITM/revocation/leak tests, and it adds a Desktop page, a CLI and secrets through get_secret.
reads.worst: It needs Python 3.14 exactly and an external `nachalo` Rust wheel holding all the cryptography, so the post-quantum claims cannot be checked from this repo; the Desktop send route has no server-side confirmation.

reads.best: Novel pairing (PAKE plus safety words) where a person must send every message.
reads.worst: Unaudited draft crypto, a niche need and the public ntfy.sh relay by default.

reads.best: Real exclusive memory provider with dashboard graph, local-only host and disclosure of data and processes.
reads.worst: Windows-only, needs a separate Rust build, ships a 1.1MB generated desktop bundle and host patches, so hard to set up and review.

reads.best: Implements a real signed Ed25519 peer-pairing protocol with an explicit, documented environment allowlist for subprocess git calls so provider keys never reach the subprocess, backed by hundreds of unit/integration/e2e test files.
reads.worst: No Desktop UI of its own; everything is driven through a CLI slash command, so the polish is entirely in documentation rather than a visual surface.

reads.best: A shipped Desktop bundle implements streaming conversations, per-bot models, attachments, shortcuts and structured interactive replies with extensive interface checks.
reads.worst: File-preview routes allow most files throughout the user home via a narrow secret-name denylist, and credential lookup falls back after scoped-secret errors.

reads.best: Its middleware-level claimed replay, pins, explicit PASS/FAIL/DIVERGED/INVALID verdicts, and extensive security/test documentation make model comparison reproducible and safer.
reads.worst: The pinned code documents major untested platform limits, and replay can become INVALID or unsafe if the claim race or gateway conditions are not met.

reads.best: Tool interception and snapshot-backed synthesized reads make regression comparisons possible without a separate judge model.
reads.worst: An unclaimed replay can execute live tools before being graded INVALID, so the intended offline safety property is not guaranteed.

reads.best: A full multi-chat workflow on Hermes cron, gateway and TTS, with founder-only publishing, media-cache-confined file reads and 114 tests, including security suites.
reads.worst: Needs gateway setup across many group chats, has no screenshots or demo, and writes helper scripts into HERMES_HOME/scripts.

reads.best: Session-and-task-bound proof receipts, scoped checks and extensive adversarial tests make worker accountability concrete.
reads.worst: Repeated trivial checks can earn trust and an earlier passing receipt survives later failures, so the policy cannot establish task quality.

reads.best: Profile delivery is gated on revision-bound native task evidence, with source-passage checks, library freshness tracking and substantial mechanics and integration tests.
reads.worst: Specialist quality still depends on extensive model-directed research and host tool execution, while passage matching and receipts cannot establish the semantic correctness of professional advice.

reads.best: A complete, 50-test pipeline from hooks to deterministic storyboard to encoded video, with ElevenLabs keys via get_secret, host-locked requests and timeouts everywhere.
reads.worst: Screenshot images are drawn into the video unredacted, and the agent can pick paid ElevenLabs narration through the tool without the confirmation the Desktop asks for.

reads.best: A full Desktop UI over Hermes's own automation, with atomic writes, confined paths, credential redaction, 94 backend tests and screenshots.
reads.worst: Imports Hermes internals (cron.jobs), the conflict check on whole-skill saves is optional, and script editing through the dashboard API is effectively code execution.

reads.best: It turns persistent owner constraints into deterministic hooks that can block unsafe actions instead of merely reminding the model.
reads.worst: Its bounded shell-command parser cannot understand inline scripts or every indirect mutation, leaving documented enforcement gaps.

reads.best: Finished like a product: many screenshots, a large Desktop and dashboard UI, and a safety design where nothing is deleted without a frozen, re-checked review list and a 30-day Trash.
reads.worst: About 9,000 lines of code that deletes files, prunes sessions and stops processes, and not one test is in the repository.

reads.best: It converts per-tool safety policy into host-enforced behavior that prompts cannot reliably guarantee, while retaining an audit trail.
reads.worst: The small package has no Desktop surface and its fail-open hook-error behavior weakens the safety promise in damaged configurations.

reads.best: Closed cache roots, snapshot revalidation, fresh approval receipts, Desktop planning and extensive safety tests make destructive cleanup unusually deliberate.
reads.worst: macOS-only cleanup remains irreversible and nontransactional; regeneration costs are estimates and concurrent cache activity can interrupt execution.

reads.best: It adds a substantive defense layer to Hermes execution, including hard rules, review of actual script bytes, operator escalation, and extensive regression cases.
reads.worst: It depends on private terminal internals and external model judgment, increasing maintenance and privacy risks while script contents are sent to the configured model.

reads.best: Native accessible controls, focus restoration, SDK-only navigation and Node/browser tests solve a concrete Desktop accessibility problem.
reads.worst: It searches only the creation-ordered first 500 fetched sessions, Ctrl+H can lose to core handling, and real screen-reader acceptance remains unverified.

reads.best: It implements a polished, real multi-session browser canvas with CDP frames, telemetry, and a tested human 2FA handoff.
reads.worst: Its agent tools still expose unrestricted browser clicking and page JavaScript, with no code-enforced approval or handoff gate for sensitive actions.

reads.best: Quote-checked evidence, persisted verdicts, computed effort/calendar estimates and focused offline tests enforce useful planning discipline.
reads.worst: A failed or malformed independent verifier is stored as skipped and still satisfies the briefing freshness gate, so a plan can advance without a successful independent check.

reads.best: A substantial hardware engine and editable multi-device UI integrate live controls, modulation and recording.
reads.worst: The chat endpoint obtains raw provider credentials through resolve_runtime_provider and constructs subscription Authorization headers instead of using the catalog-required credentialed_provider_request route.

reads.best: The code separates explicit feedback from tentative hypotheses and builds inspectable, sourced recommendation paths.
reads.worst: The workflow asks the agent to coordinate ten tools and research steps, which adds setup and execution complexity.

reads.best: A real guard that only a plugin can add: it classifies calls by content, caps its time budget inside Hermes's callback timeout, escalates rather than allows on error, and ships per-gate tests and an SSRF fetch guard.
reads.worst: Its value is mostly for agents that touch EVM wallets, its injection scoring is heuristic, and as its README admits, a WARN is auto-approved on unattended surfaces (cron, --yolo).

reads.best: Conversation-specific routing, compaction/deletion handling, acknowledgement after delivery and cancellation-aware waits go well beyond an MCP messaging wrapper ([code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/koshikraj/birdie/fa9c7a13bd7733ec990942a835b915d0ab21cd28/integrations/hermes/__init__.py), [tests](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/koshikraj/birdie/fa9c7a13bd7733ec990942a835b915d0ab21cd28/integrations/hermes/test_plugin.py)).
reads.worst: It requires a separate running bus and setup step; conversations become reachable only after a turn and again need a turn after restart, limiting always-on availability ([lifecycle](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/koshikraj/birdie/fa9c7a13bd7733ec990942a835b915d0ab21cd28/integrations/hermes/__init__.py)).

reads.best: Native TTS integration uses profile-scoped secrets, schema-aware validation, bounded polling, no automatic paid-job retries and offline transport/provider tests.
reads.worst: Requires paid GMI service, lacks streaming and voice-bubble support, and invokes chargeable generation without a separate approval prompt.

reads.best: Combines tracked work, adversarial review and validated, hash-checked CAD tool outputs while exposing unmeasured engineering gaps.
reads.worst: Its own pinned documentation admits failed reviewer calibration, checks that cannot establish some claimed requirements, and several-million-token demonstration cost.

reads.best: Read-only by construction with no dependencies, every answer carrying its block, 114 tests with CI, and documentation that publishes a measurement showing its own hook does not save model calls.
reads.worst: It is a crypto-only niche that leans on public RPC and price endpoints, its context hook's keyword gate fires on common words such as 'base', 'swap' or 'portfolio', and its catalog pull request is closed.

reads.best: Uses measured tool-loop activity and SQLite history to turn effort estimates into a feedback loop with no external service.
reads.worst: Participation still depends on a prompt the model can ignore, and wall-clock measurements include approval delays while excluding delegated subagent calls.

reads.best: The most finished product of the batch: a full React Desktop sidebar UI, dashboard backend, screenshot, and SSRF/path-traversal hardening on its own enrichment fetches, despite its secrets-sounding name holding no credentials at all.
reads.worst: No automated test suite exists anywhere in the repository, unlike comparable entries.

reads.best: Source-quote validation, explicit review, stale-result protection and saved-appearance verification make a useful document workflow unusually concrete.
reads.worst: The supported input range is narrow: printable ASCII AcroForms only, with no OCR, radio groups or signing, and retained packet data has no cleanup interface.

reads.best: The PDF engine is unusually conservative about unsupported forms, source quotes, and explicit user review before export.
reads.worst: The pinned tree lacks a manifest, README, tests, and the promised Desktop workspace implementation, making the submission incomplete as a catalog plugin.

reads.best: A real new model backend for Hermes with about 729 tests against a fake ACP server and CI on Linux and Windows.
reads.worst: It auto-approves the Google agent's native file edits and shell commands, bypassing Hermes terminal approval with no switch, and its own status table says real auth and inference are unverified for this release.

reads.best: Careful engineering: native OAuth, terms re-checked against human approval before accept/submit, idempotent envelopes and a large test suite.
reads.worst: Only useful to SPAWN marketplace workers, and its own README says it is a development preview with live acceptance incomplete and a private repository.

reads.best: A fresh idea, holding the agent to its own past claims, built carefully: private and localhost addresses refused even after DNS or redirects, background checks, and context injected once per change.
reads.worst: Claims are spotted by sentence regex, so it misses deploys described differently, and it only re-checks at session start or from a cron command the user must set up.

reads.best: Generation-aware device control, bounded private-network discovery and stateful device-stub tests make the hardware integration concrete.
reads.worst: The chat settings loader omits allow_model_sweep, so enabling that documented setting never reaches the handler through ctx.get_config.

reads.best: The compact find/details/call interface gives Hermes broad live-data reach without flooding context with hundreds of separate tool definitions.
reads.worst: Nearly all value and reliability are delegated to an external paid service outside the pinned code, with no local implementation or tests to inspect.

reads.best: Reducing repeated model work through recorded execution evidence and scheduler integration directly improves the user’s agent.
reads.worst: Command flattening discards working directories and timeouts, and generated scripts assume exit zero rather than preserving recorded exit assertions, weakening the claimed equivalence.

reads.best: Substantial local retrieval code includes WAL-aware snapshotting, incremental sync, locks, structured errors and tests built from synthetic Zotero libraries.
reads.worst: Search and its strong/thin/none coverage verdict are lexical term-count heuristics, so relevant synonyms can be missed and coverage is not evidence quality.

reads.best: Signed receipts with content-free stubs and concurrency tests make agent activity independently inspectable.
reads.worst: It reads its private signing key from a local PEM file rather than Hermes secrets, and local key access permits rewriting the audit history.

reads.best: Dry-run-with-diff approval is a fresh idea that changes where Hermes executes commands.
reads.worst: Admits it is not isolation (host process, best-effort guards), the sandbox tests are underscore-named and not collected, and approval happens in an external script, not in Hermes.

reads.best: Complete stdlib tool set with persistent watchlist, a /pm command and automation blueprints, plus a 24KB test file.
reads.worst: A niche audience, and the data is public Polymarket API calls a script could do.

reads.best: The integration follows run state, reports failed or cancelled work, and provides plan, run, status, and cancellation tools ([source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jigjoy-ai/hermes-baro/79cb40f9baf20529e4587f07653d31ea2654bf41/tools.py)).
reads.worst: The launch approval names only a configured backend although tool arguments can select a remote model endpoint, leaving the actual data recipient undisclosed ([source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jigjoy-ai/hermes-baro/79cb40f9baf20529e4587f07653d31ea2654bf41/core/consent.py)).

reads.best: Bootstrap token is read only via Hermes's own secret-source environment API, marked protected, and the plugin explicitly never touches .env or auth.json.
reads.worst: Only 3 test functions; KV v1 fallback, namespace headers, HTTP error codes and the response-size cap are all implemented but untested.

reads.best: Carefully scoped safety design: loopback-only GET/HEAD with no redirects, auth headers rejected and redacted, promotion behind Hermes's approval hook with a SHA-256 re-check, plus ADRs, SECURITY.md and CI.
reads.worst: The loopback check compares hostnames, not resolved IPs, and there are no tests for the diff rules, promotion or live-transport safety checks the README says are tested.

reads.best: Checks real workspace changes, tool usage and token consumption rather than relying on the agent’s assertion of success.
reads.worst: The runner unconditionally starts Hermes with --yolo without a sandbox or approval gate, violating the catalog’s child-process approval rule.

reads.best: Useful computation beyond chat: resumable cached analysis, RAW/JPEG pairing, disk checks and partial-failure tests support a practical photo workflow.
reads.worst: Image metrics cannot tell whether the subject is sharp or eyes are closed; that requires a separately requested Hermes vision check, and RAW quality depends on embedded previews.

reads.best: Deterministic parsers, explicit warnings instead of guesses, input protection, and focused tests make the safety-critical path trustworthy.
reads.worst: It is a specialized file tool without Hermes hooks, Desktop, or broader agent-platform changes, and PDF/image support has format limits.

reads.best: Fully offline, standard-library code with 31 tests, month-end date rolling, per-currency totals without invented exchange rates, and quiet de-duplicated reminders.
reads.worst: A familiar subscription-tracker idea; much of it (a list plus a cron reminder) could be approximated with Hermes memory and a scheduled prompt.

reads.best: Uses real editable video projects, source hashes, idempotent queue requests, and uncertain-delivery handling instead of claiming a render succeeded.
reads.worst: Setup depends on a separate editor, speech model and private reviewed recipe; the complete new-footage attachment-to-reply-edit loop is not verified.

reads.best: The archive importer validates ZIP contents, reports per-file coverage, and has a substantial offline test suite.
reads.worst: Only four JSON shapes are parsed, and the evidence tool records consent metadata without sending evidence to a provider.

reads.best: Validated argv, third-party-package checks, shared-UID refusal, fresh approval keys and after-state policy verification make a focused hardware tool.
reads.worst: Live evidence is read-only and OEM network counters vary; the subprocess output cap is checked after capture_output has already buffered the response.

reads.best: It never imports candidate code in its audit, fails closed, and is backed by about 213 tests and two CI workflows; it contains no text aimed at steering a judge.
reads.worst: It is tied to this one hackathon (the Nov 11 deadline and rule snapshots are hard-coded), most of its 33 requirement rows are manual checklist items, and its catalog pull request is closed.

reads.best: Spend-aware manifest: server marked untrusted with declared per-tool costs and a per-chat spend limit so paid calls need approval.
reads.worst: No code of its own: all the work is in a third-party npx package fetched at launch, and the pinned commit has no tests.

reads.best: The pinned package declares its key as a Hermes secret, marks the server untrusted for approvals, and documents public output and constrained photo uploads. [Source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MrHydeDev/openwall-mcp-plugin/26e25c7a0acf880cdc5bbec86a1b592318a5f885/plugin.json)
reads.worst: The creative drawing behavior is entirely in an unpublished remote server outside the pin, leaving only configuration and workflow guidance reviewable. [Source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MrHydeDev/openwall-mcp-plugin/26e25c7a0acf880cdc5bbec86a1b592318a5f885/README.md)

reads.best: The adapter includes extensive lifecycle tests, a fully locked npm tree, scrubbed child environments and owned-process cleanup.
reads.worst: A thin integration around an existing pet requires Node plus large runtime and Electron downloads, and only Windows has been verified.

reads.best: Uses Hermes provider and PKCE seams instead of implementing credential storage or inference transport itself.
reads.worst: The pinned repository contains no tests despite the PR describing an external contract suite, and custom auth URL validation does not require HTTPS.

reads.best: Fits Hermes’s web-provider interface with secret-scope credentials, engine validation, per-URL errors, and mocked contract tests.
reads.worst: The PR reports no live API or local Hermes-validator check, and requests are sequential with a 120-second timeout each and unbounded response reads.

reads.best: The tools compute and rank cross-cultural differences locally, with country lookup, task weighting, input handling, and tests covering data and calculations.
reads.worst: Country scores and advice are author-encoded approximations with limited country-level source traceability, so confident-looking comparisons may overstate their evidence.

reads.best: A bundled offline catalog, practical input validation and handler tests make style discovery accessible through both tools and Desktop.
reads.worst: Its core output is a substituted prompt template; building or rendering the actual animation is left to other tools or skills.

reads.best: End-to-end pipeline in one ce_run call, with safe-name checks and tests.
reads.worst: Scoring and copy are deterministic keyword heuristics, weaker than what the README's pitch suggests.

reads.best: The scan subprocess is run with an explicitly minimized environment (only PATH/HOME/LANG/INSTALL_DIR) specifically to avoid leaking provider API keys, and this is directly unit-tested.
reads.worst: The actual scanning logic is delegated entirely to an external bridge project not bundled in this repo, so this plugin is mostly a thin wrapper and alert-injection layer around someone else's tool.

reads.best: State-changing repairs request Hermes human approval in addition to a plan/confirm step, allowlisted verbs, and a persistent repair budget. (Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Megumiiiiii/hermes-nurse/a830f7c8a71490c69368cf2071b85b4476e561b0/hermes_nurse/repair.py; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Megumiiiiii/hermes-nurse/a830f7c8a71490c69368cf2071b85b4476e561b0/README.md)
reads.worst: The crash-loop rate divides the cumulative pm2 restart count by the current process uptime, so historical restarts can still falsely block a healthy service; ledger updates also lack locking. (Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Megumiiiiii/hermes-nurse/a830f7c8a71490c69368cf2071b85b4476e561b0/hermes_nurse/repair.py)

reads.best: Policy-changing model calls require approval and the ledger associates pending payments with individual tool-call IDs.
reads.worst: Payment recognition is heuristic, unexpected pre-hook errors fail open, and pending payments do not reserve daily budget before concurrent calls execute.

reads.best: A compact read-only registry implementation avoids executing uninstallers and includes fake-registry, non-Windows import and live-test coverage.
reads.worst: It only inventories registry-registered Windows software, and same-name entries collapse into a first-view summary that can hide version differences.

reads.best: The inspect-change-measure workflow includes dry-run diffs, prompt backups and measured time to first audio.
reads.worst: convai_client.api_key falls back to raw os.environ even when the profile secret is empty, and voice-test overrides mutate live agent settings without the apply gate advertised for every write.

reads.best: OAuth with PKCE and an untrusted MCP marking, so no stored secret and writes need approval.
reads.worst: No code or tests, and its 550-line skill tells the agent to reach for Weir proactively and to re-download the skill from a remote URL.

reads.best: Careful privacy (hashed ids, no raw content stored) with tests and a demo.
reads.worst: Mostly a formatting layer that a skill or prompt could largely reproduce.

reads.best: The connector and skill expose a focused design-to-code workflow with clear credit and data disclosures.
reads.worst: Only manifests and a skill are pinned; the closed hosted capture implementation and runtime tool behavior cannot be inspected or tested from this repository.

reads.best: The compact package declares its secret through Hermes and documents installation, write permissions and missing mention wakeups candidly.
reads.worst: Its implementation is a config-and-skill wrapper around npm code outside the Git pin, with default trust allowing posting without confirmation.

reads.best: A polished hosted creative service with OAuth sign-in and no keys to paste.
reads.worst: There is no plugin code, only config files and a 20 KB skill for a remote paid service that does not appear at the pinned commit, and it is generic across many agents rather than made for Hermes.

reads.best: The package marks the server untrusted and includes a small contract smoke test plus explicit payment and tipping consent guidance.
reads.worst: The pinned package contains no Reader implementation, and its smoke test checks discovery rather than article, payment or failure behavior.

reads.best: A small standard-library integration exposes fourteen practical agent-control operations and reads its token through Hermes secrets.
reads.worst: The model can request full-auto permission mode through an ungated RPC wrapper; validation is delegated to the external daemon and the included selftest only drives a mock.

reads.best: The untrusted MCP declaration preserves write approvals, and the documentation clearly discloses contact changes that can trigger emails or automations.
reads.worst: Only two configuration files are submitted, without server code or tests, and the bundled bridge keeps OAuth tokens in ~/.mcp-auth rather than Hermes’s secret store.

reads.best: The invoice and cancellation workflows explicitly require previews and confirmation tokens, and the manifest marks the remote server untrusted.
reads.worst: No server implementation or automated tests are pinned, and the npx OAuth bridge stores tokens in ~/.mcp-auth rather than Hermes’s own store.

reads.best: No-key access to nonprofit records has a clear research use, and the skills distinguish missing public data from zero values.
reads.worst: Only client configuration and skills are pinned: the server implementation, data processing and tool behavior cannot be inspected or tested from this repository.

reads.best: The small keyless connector clearly discloses remote processing and the limits of its reference dataset.
reads.worst: The pinned package contains no service implementation or tests; its seven remotely supplied tools can change outside the reviewed commit.

reads.best: A small readable connector marks the server untrusted, while the skill describes spending limits and idempotent paid-call retries.
reads.worst: The pinned package has no server implementation or tests and its README supplies other-client setup rather than a Hermes authentication flow; the Hermes MCP entry includes neither OAuth configuration nor access-key wiring.

reads.best: The library separates host authorization from agent decisions and includes substantial lifecycle, audit and authorization tests.
reads.worst: The pinned plugin subdirectory imports a sibling implementation package absent from that install layout, catches registration failure, and supplies no active Guard service; the PR explicitly confirms zero registered hooks for that layout.

reads.best: bracket.py is a real 1,235-line state machine that deals strategy cards, pairs matches and tracks verdicts under .arena/.
reads.worst: It is a skill bundle whose manifest says it was "generated from" another author's repo, with a 13-line README, no tests, no Hermes plugin code and a default of 100 agents (hundreds of sub-agent calls).

reads.best: A consistent bridge exposes public profile research and authenticated inbox operations through ordinary Hermes tool schemas.
reads.worst: The required engine is absent from the pinned repository, has no bundled tests, and receives an Instagram session-file path instead of Hermes-managed credentials.

reads.best: It is compact, local-only, and persists state without model calls or prompt-cache changes.
reads.worst: Its keyword rules are a shallow personality prompt and the delivered test is an assertion script rather than a comprehensive suite.

reads.best: The installer offers both local-server and Docker registration paths, and the README distinguishes test coins from real BSV.
reads.worst: No native entrypoint or portable MCP package is shipped, the setup key is not executed by Hermes, and manual installation defaults to an unpinned latest image without a declared untrusted spending gate.

reads.best: Wide platform coverage with key in a secret-typed config field.
reads.worst: Mostly skills plus a remote MCP URL, no plugin code or tests; pinned commit was not fetchable so it was scored from main.

reads.best: Declares its tools, a Desktop entry and settings cleanly in a full manifest.
reads.worst: Claims more than the code does: inspect_surface ignores target_url and always returns mock_surface_scene data, and there is no CDP connection at all, so the agent gets invented defects and source lines.

reads.best: The PR describes a potentially useful reproducible-session workflow, whose implementation remains unverified.
